title: Building a CD Ladder When 12-Month CDs Pay the Most
description: FDIC national averages as of August 17, 2026 put 12-month CDs at 1.71% APY, above every longer term. How to build a four-rung ladder around that.
content:
The FDIC's national deposit rate table has a shape right now that breaks the rule most people learned about CDs. The 12-month average sits at 1.71% APY. Go out to 24 months and the average drops to 1.57%. At 36 months it's 1.34%, at 48 months 1.27%, and at 60 months 1.36% — still below the one-year figure. Those are national averages as of August 17, 2026, and the direction of travel is the point: on average, banks are not paying you extra to commit money for longer.

That matters because the ladder structure most primers describe assumes the opposite. The classic version tells you to buy CDs at one, two, three, and four years, then roll each maturing rung into a new four-year CD, because the long end pays the most and staggering the maturities gives you regular access. Feed today's numbers into that structure and you're taking your lowest yields on the money you can touch least.

## The shape of the curve right now

Here is the full FDIC national average CD table, plus savings and money market for comparison, all as of August 17, 2026:

| Product | National average APY |
|---|---|
| Savings | 0.38% |
| Money market | 0.63% |
| 1 month CD | 0.22% |
| 3 month CD | 1.14% |
| 6 month CD | 1.41% |
| 12 month CD | 1.71% |
| 24 month CD | 1.57% |
| 36 month CD | 1.34% |
| 48 month CD | 1.27% |
| 60 month CD | 1.36% |

Read it top to bottom and the curve climbs steeply from one month to twelve, peaks, then slides back down through four years before ticking up slightly at five. A curve that rises and then falls like this gets called flat-to-inverted. The premium you'd normally collect for term risk has gone missing past the one-year mark.

Two cautions before you build anything on this table. First, an average has institutions on both sides of it, so some banks pay well above every figure here and some pay well below. Check your own institution's rate sheet rather than assuming these levels apply to you. Second, the product mix behind each tenor differs, so the small 60-month uptick is not necessarily a signal about five-year money. Use this table for the shape, not the levels.

## The break-even on locking long

Say you're choosing between a 48-month CD at the 1.27% average and a 12-month CD at 1.71%, with a plan to reinvest the 12-month CD three more times.

Over four years the 48-month CD compounds to about 5.18% total on your principal — that's 1.0127 to the fourth power. The rolling plan earns 1.71% in year one, then whatever three more one-year renewals bring. Solve for the renewal rate that makes the two tie and you get roughly **1.12% per year**. Do it with simple interest instead of compounding and the answer barely moves — about 1.12% either way.

So the question isn't whether rates fall. It's narrower: would 12-month CDs have to average below about 1.12% for the next three years? That's a drop of nearly 0.6 points from today's average, sustained for three years. It might happen. But notice the price of that insurance — 0.44 points a year of current yield, on money you can't reach — and notice that it only pays off in a fairly specific scenario. Locking long isn't wrong here. It's just no longer free, which is exactly what a flat curve means.

## A four-rung ladder for a front-loaded curve

Take $24,000 and split it into four equal $6,000 rungs. Compare two structures at the national averages.

**The classic long ladder** — 12, 24, 36, and 48 months:

- 12 month at 1.71% → $102.60 of first-year interest
- 24 month at 1.57% → $94.20
- 36 month at 1.34% → $80.40
- 48 month at 1.27% → $76.20
- First-year interest: **$353.40**, a blended 1.4725%

The 24-, 36-, and 48-month rungs hold those rates for their full terms. The 12-month rung does not — it matures after year one and gets reinvested at whatever the curve offers then, exactly like the shorter ladder's rungs.

**A front-loaded ladder** — 3, 6, 12, and 24 months — can't be totaled without stating an assumption, because two of its rungs mature inside the first year and have to be reinvested. Assume the plan laid out in the next section: each rung rolls into a 12-month CD as it comes due, and the 12-month average is still near 1.71% when it does.

- 3 month at 1.14% earns $17.10, then $6,017.10 earns 1.71% for nine months → $94.27 for the year
- 6 month at 1.41% earns $42.30, then $6,042.30 earns 1.71% for six months → $93.96
- 12 month at 1.71% → $102.60
- 24 month at 1.57% → $94.20 accrued in year one
- First-year interest: **$385.03**, a blended 1.6043%

On that assumption the front-loaded ladder beats the classic one by $31.63 in the first year, and it does it while handing you cash in month 3 instead of month 12.

The assumption is doing real work there, so test it against a worse one. Suppose the reinvestment rates available at months 3 and 6 were today's *short* averages instead — 1.14% and 1.41%. Then the 3-month rung earns $68.55 across the year, the 6-month rung earns $84.90, and the total falls to $350.24, a blended 1.4594%. The classic ladder wins that scenario by $3.16 over the year. That is 26 cents a month, in exchange for locking $12,000 away until 2029 and 2030.

So the honest range runs from beating the long ladder by $31.63 to losing to it by $3.16 — and the losing case still leaves you with a maturity every three to six months. The downside of staying short, on these averages, is small enough to measure in cents. A single 24-month rung stays in as a partial hedge: if one-year rates do slide, that rung holds 1.57% while everything shorter re-prices.

## Rolling each rung at maturity

The plan is to convert every rung into a 12-month CD as it comes due, so that after two years you own four rolling one-year CDs sitting at the tenor the curve pays best.

**Month 3.** The 3-month rung matures with about $17.10 of interest. Roll $6,017.10 into a 12-month CD, which now matures in month 15.

**Month 6.** The 6-month rung matures with about $42.30. Roll $6,042.30 into a 12-month CD maturing in month 18.

**Month 12.** The original 12-month rung matures with $102.60. Roll the full $6,102.60 forward again, maturing month 24.

**Month 24.** Two separate rungs come due this month. The original 24-month rung matures with about $189.88 of compounded interest on its $6,000. The rung you rolled at month 12 is a different amount: one year at 1.71% on $6,102.60 is about $104.35. Two maturities landing in the same month is a real scheduling flaw, and it's worth fixing rather than ignoring — when you roll at month 12, use a 9-month or 15-month term if your bank offers one, which re-spaces that rung to month 21 or 27 and restores the gaps.

From there the ladder self-maintains. Each maturity is a decision point where you look at the current curve, not a mechanical renewal. If the 24-month rate has climbed above the 12-month by then, extend. And find the length of your bank's automatic-renewal grace period in the disclosure — that window after maturity is when you can move the money without a penalty.

## The cost of breaking a rung early

Here's why term choice deserves the attention. A CD's early-withdrawal penalty is set in its disclosure and is often quoted as a number of months of interest.

Take the 48-month rung: $6,000 at 1.27% earns $76.20 a year, or $6.35 a month. Suppose you need the money after eight months and the penalty is six months of interest.

- Interest earned in eight months: $50.80
- Penalty: $38.10
- Net to you: **$12.70**

That's 0.21% over eight months, or about 0.32% annualized — less than the 0.38% savings average, and roughly half the money market average. Break it earlier still and the penalty can exceed what the CD has earned, at which point the shortfall comes out of principal. Penalty terms vary by bank and by term length, so the disclosure is the only place to check.

The lesson isn't that penalties are unfair. It's that a CD's stated APY is only what you earn if you hold it to maturity. Money that might be needed belongs in an emergency fund built from liquid accounts, not in a rung you'll break.

## FDIC coverage across a multi-bank ladder

Chasing the best rate at each tenor often means several banks, which is fine and sometimes changes your insurance math. FDIC coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Credit unions carry NCUA coverage instead, on similar terms.

A $24,000 ladder isn't near any limit. But a $900,000 ladder might be, and the fix is straightforward: spreading it across four banks gives each account its own $250,000 of coverage, and different ownership categories at the same bank — single, joint, certain revocable trusts — are insured separately from each other. The easy thing to miss is accrued interest. Coverage applies to principal plus interest earned, so a rung funded right at $250,000 will be uninsured on its interest by maturity. Leave headroom.

## A checklist before the first rung

- Plot this same curve from your own bank's rate sheet. National averages tell you the shape; only your bank tells you your rate.
- Compare the 12-month CD to your existing savings rate. If savings is close, you're paying a lock-up for very little — and savings floats while a CD doesn't.
- Read the early-withdrawal penalty for each term before funding, not after.
- Check whether automatic renewal is on by default, and write every maturity date on a calendar. A ladder nobody tracks becomes a pile of auto-renewed CDs at whatever rate the bank picks.

Remember that APY already accounts for compounding while a quoted interest rate does not, so compare APY to APY. And treat the current curve as information about today, not a forecast. The reason a front-loaded ladder makes sense right now is not that anyone knows where rates are heading. It's that the long end isn't paying you enough to care.

*Rate figures cited are FDIC national averages as of August 17, 2026. Averages are not offers, and rates at individual institutions differ substantially.*

title: The Real Cost of Leaving Extra Cash in Your Checking Account
description: FDIC national averages as of August 17, 2026: interest checking 0.07% APY vs money market 0.63%. How to size a checking buffer and move the rest.
content:
Your checking account is doing a job, and paying you is not part of it. As of August 17, 2026, the FDIC national average for interest checking is 0.07% APY. Savings averages 0.38%. Money market accounts average 0.63%. Those are national averages across thousands of insured institutions, so individual accounts sit on both sides of each figure — but in that snapshot, the account you touch most often is the one paying you the least.

The standard advice stops at "don't keep too much in checking," which is useless without a number attached. This post gives you the number. You'll get a method for calculating how much cash genuinely has to sit in checking to cover your month, the arithmetic on what the excess costs, and the settlement details — cutoff times, business days, holds — that quietly push people into carrying a far fatter checking balance than they need.

One thing before the math. The goal is not to squeeze checking down to zero. A buffer that's too thin can cost you more in a single overdraft or returned-payment fee than a year of extra yield on a few thousand dollars will earn. What you want is a deliberate number, sized to your own payment calendar, not a vague instinct that you should "probably move some over."

## Why Checking Pays So Little

Checking is an operations account. It clears debit swipes, absorbs autopay, holds direct deposit, and settles checks on days you can't predict. The usual explanation for the low rate is that banks treat checking as a service rather than as a way to raise funding, and you can see part of that logic from your own side of the counter: moving a checking account means rewiring direct deposit, updating every merchant that has your account number, and living through a few weeks of overlap.

You don't have to accept anyone's theory about why the gap exists, though. The verifiable part is what your own statement says. Look up the APY your checking account actually pays, compare it to the averages above, and treat the difference as the number that matters.

Worth knowing: the 0.07% figure is the average across *interest-bearing* checking accounts. Plenty of checking accounts pay nothing at all. If yours is one of them, the gap you're looking at isn't 0.31 or 0.56 percentage points — it's the full 0.38% or 0.63%.

## The Gap in Dollars

Take a household carrying $18,000 in checking, which turns out to be about $15,000 more than the month actually requires. APY already accounts for compounding, so multiplying a balance by the APY gives you roughly a year's interest if the balance stays put.

At the FDIC national averages as of August 17, 2026:

- **Checking at 0.07%:** $15,000 × 0.0007 = **$10.50 a year**
- **Savings at 0.38%:** $15,000 × 0.0038 = **$57.00 a year** — a gain of $46.50
- **Money market at 0.63%:** $15,000 × 0.0063 = **$94.50 a year** — a gain of $84.00
- **12-month CD at 1.71%:** $15,000 × 0.0171 = **$256.50 a year** — a gain of $246.00, with the money locked up and an early-withdrawal penalty if you break it

Eighty-four dollars a year is seven dollars a month. That is honest arithmetic on national averages, and it's fair to say it's not life-changing. But two things scale it up. First, an average has accounts sitting on both sides of it, so run the numbers again using the rate you are actually offered rather than the national figure — each additional full percentage point on $15,000 works out to another $150 a year. Second, this is a one-time setup that keeps paying. The transfer takes an afternoon; the yield difference recurs for as long as the balance sits there.

## Sizing the Working Buffer

Your checking balance should cover the longest stretch between incoming deposits, plus a cushion for the bills that vary. Here's the count, using a household spending $4,500 a month — $3,100 in fixed obligations (rent, insurance, utilities, subscriptions, card autopay) and about $1,400 in variable spending.

**Step 1 — Daily burn.** $4,500 ÷ 30 = **$150 a day**.

**Step 2 — Longest deposit gap.** Paid on the 1st and the 15th, the longest stretch between deposits runs about 16 days. $150 × 16 = **$2,400**.

**Step 3 — Variance cushion.** Add 25% for the months when the utility bill spikes or an annual premium lands. $2,400 × 1.25 = **$3,000**.

**Step 4 — Floor check.** If your bank waives its monthly fee only above a minimum balance, use the higher of that minimum and your calculated buffer. Don't earn $84 to pay a maintenance fee.

So: $3,000 stays, $15,000 moves. Rebuild the count if your income is irregular. Freelancers and commission earners should size the gap to the longest realistic dry spell, not the average one, and should expect a bigger checking buffer than a salaried household needs. That's not inefficiency; that's paying for the ability to sleep.

Note that this buffer is separate from an emergency fund. The buffer covers timing. The emergency fund covers events, and it belongs in the higher-yield account alongside the rest of the swept cash.

## Settlement Mechanics That Keep Cash Stuck

This is the part that actually causes over-funded checking accounts. People aren't ignorant of rates. They've been burned once by a transfer that took longer than expected, and they've been padding ever since.

**Business days are not calendar days.** ACH transfers between banks typically settle in one to three business days. Weekends and federal holidays don't count. A transfer you start Friday evening can post Tuesday, or Wednesday if Monday is a holiday.

**Cutoff times.** Institutions set a daily cutoff. Submit after it and your transfer is dated the next business day before the settlement clock even starts. Find yours and write it down.

**Push versus pull matters.** Initiating a transfer *from* the receiving bank (pulling) and initiating it *from* the sending bank (pushing) can run on different timelines and different hold policies, even between the same two accounts. Try both directions once with a small amount and record how many days each actually took.

**Holds on incoming deposits.** Money that has arrived is not always money you can spend. A deposit into a savings account may face an availability hold before it can be withdrawn again, which makes the return trip slower than the outbound one.

**Trailing debits.** A debit card authorization can post days after you swipe. Restaurant tips, gas station holds, and hotel authorizations settle on their own schedule. Checks you mailed clear whenever the recipient gets around to depositing them.

**Transfer limits still exist.** Regulation D's six-transfer-per-month limit on savings and money market accounts was suspended in 2020, but plenty of banks kept their own limits in place. Check whether yours does before you plan on frequent moves in both directions.

The fix isn't to keep an extra month in checking. It's to size the buffer to the slowest settlement window you've personally measured, and to make the return trip a known quantity rather than a gamble.

## Where the Swept Cash Belongs

| Account type | FDIC national average APY (as of Aug 17, 2026) | Best role |
|---|---|---|
| Interest checking | 0.07% | Bills, debit, the working buffer only |
| Savings | 0.38% | Buffer overflow and emergency fund |
| Money market | 0.63% | Same role, often with check or debit access |
| 3-month CD | 1.14% | Money with a known near-term date |
| 12-month CD | 1.71% | Money you're confident you won't touch |

The money market average sitting above the savings average is a fact about this snapshot, not a permanent law of nature, so compare the two directly whenever you open something new. One distinction to keep straight: a money market *deposit account* at a bank is FDIC-insured; a money market *mutual fund* at a brokerage is not.

If sweeping means opening an account at a second institution, that's a small side benefit. FDIC coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, so spreading balances across two banks raises your total covered amount. Credit unions are insured by the NCUA rather than the FDIC, at the same standard limit.

## When Sweeping Isn't Worth It

Skip it, or do it lightly, in these cases:

- **The excess is small.** On $2,000, the checking-to-money-market gap at national averages is about $11 a year. One overdraft fee erases years of that.
- **Your income timing is genuinely unpredictable.** Pay for the certainty. A larger buffer is a reasonable purchase.
- **Your checking account has a balance-based fee waiver.** Dropping below the threshold to chase a few dollars of yield is a losing trade.
- **You'd be tempted to overcorrect.** If moving money makes you likely to cut the buffer to the bone and then scramble, the yield isn't worth the stress.

## A Routine That Survives Busy Months

Automate the outbound leg and leave the return leg manual. Set a recurring transfer for the day after each payday — modest enough that it never threatens the buffer — so accumulation happens whether or not you're paying attention. Pulling money back should require a deliberate decision, which is exactly the friction you want.

Then review the buffer twice a year, or whenever a fixed cost changes materially: a new lease, a car payment ending, a switch from biweekly to semi-monthly pay. Buffers drift upward on their own if nobody checks them.

## Where to Start

Open your last three months of checking statements and find the lowest balance in each month. If that floor sits consistently higher than your calculated buffer, the difference is what's been sitting idle, and you now know roughly what it's costing you at the national averages above.

Then run the small test transfer out and back, and size your buffer to the number of business days it actually took rather than to the worst thing you can imagine. Once you have a real figure instead of a fear, the rest of the cash is free to go somewhere it earns.

title: How FDIC Ownership Categories Stack Coverage at One Bank
description: Single, joint, trust, and retirement accounts each carry a separate FDIC limit at the same bank, and here is how to stack and verify them.
content:
The $250,000 figure gets repeated so often that most people treat it as a hard ceiling on what any one bank can safely hold for them. It isn't. The full sentence matters: FDIC coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. That last clause is the part doing the real work, and it is the part almost nobody reads closely.

Ownership categories are not a loophole. They are the FDIC's method of answering a specific question during a bank failure: who owned this money, and who was supposed to benefit from it? Accounts that answer that question differently get counted separately. A household that understands the categories can hold well past $250,000 at a single institution with every dollar insured, without opening accounts at five different banks or chasing paperwork tricks.

Below: how the four categories most households use are calculated, a worked example with the arithmetic spelled out, the moves that feel like they should add coverage but don't, and how to verify your own numbers in the FDIC's own tools.

## Coverage Per Category, Not Per Account

Within a single ownership category at a single bank, every deposit you hold gets added together and measured against one $250,000 limit. Product type is irrelevant to that math. A savings account, a money market account, and three CDs held in your name alone are not five separate limits — they are one balance, tested once.

Move to a different ownership category and the counter resets. That is the entire mechanism. Coverage includes principal plus interest accrued through the date a bank fails, so a balance sitting just under the line can drift over it as interest posts.

Deposits are what's covered. Mutual funds, stocks, bonds, annuities, and crypto bought through a bank or its affiliated brokerage carry no FDIC insurance regardless of where you purchased them. Credit unions are outside the FDIC system entirely; they are insured by the NCUA, which applies a parallel $250,000 structure through a different fund and a different agency.

The FDIC recognizes several ownership categories, including ones for businesses, government entities, and employee benefit plans. Four cover almost every household situation.

## The Four Categories a Household Actually Uses

### Accounts in one name

Any deposit you own alone, with no co-owner and no beneficiary named, sits in the single ownership category. Everything you hold this way at one bank combines into a single $250,000 limit. Two people in the same household each get their own single-account limit at the same bank, because the category is per depositor.

### Joint accounts

A joint account gets its own limit, separate from either owner's single accounts. Each co-owner is insured up to $250,000 for their share of all joint accounts at that bank. Two owners with equal rights therefore support up to $500,000 in the joint category.

The conditions are strict and worth checking. Every co-owner must be a living person — not a business, not a trust. Each must have equal withdrawal rights. The bank's records must actually show the joint ownership. Absent a written statement otherwise, the FDIC presumes shares are equal, so a $500,000 joint balance splits $250,000 / $250,000 regardless of who deposited what.

### Trust accounts

This is the category that changed most recently, and old guidance still circulates. Since the FDIC's trust rule took effect on April 1, 2024, revocable trust deposits (payable-on-death accounts, in-trust-for accounts, and living trust accounts) and irrevocable trust deposits are combined into one trust accounts category.

The calculation is now simple: $250,000 per owner, per eligible beneficiary, capped at five beneficiaries. One owner naming three children is covered up to $750,000. Two owners naming those same three children are covered up to $1,500,000. The maximum any single owner can reach in this category at one bank is $1,250,000, and naming a sixth beneficiary adds nothing. Eligible beneficiaries are living people, charities, and nonprofit organizations.

### Certain retirement accounts

Traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs, and self-directed plan deposits combine into one $250,000 limit per owner at each bank — separate from that person's single accounts. Coverage applies to deposit products inside the account, such as an IRA CD or IRA savings account, not to securities in a brokerage IRA. Workplace plans where you don't direct the investments fall into a different category.

| Category | Who qualifies | How coverage is calculated |
|---|---|---|
| Single | One owner, no co-owner, no beneficiary | $250,000 per owner, all such deposits combined |
| Joint | Two or more living people, equal withdrawal rights | $250,000 per co-owner, shares presumed equal |
| Trust | POD, ITF, living trust, or irrevocable trust deposits | $250,000 per owner per beneficiary, five beneficiaries maximum |
| Certain retirement | IRAs and self-directed plan deposits | $250,000 per owner, all such deposits combined |

## A Worked Example: $865,000 at One Bank

Priya and Marcus hold everything at one FDIC-insured bank:

- Priya, savings in her name only: $180,000
- Marcus, savings in his name only: $95,000
- Marcus, a 12-month CD in his name only: $60,000
- Joint money market account: $400,000
- Priya's IRA CD: $130,000

Now sort by category rather than by account.

**Single accounts.** Priya's $180,000 is tested against her own $250,000 limit — insured, with $70,000 of room left. Marcus's savings and CD combine: $95,000 + $60,000 = $155,000 against his separate $250,000 limit. Insured, $95,000 of room. Note what happened there: two different products, one limit, because the ownership category is identical.

**Joint account.** $400,000 with two equal owners splits into $200,000 per owner. Each share is under $250,000, so the account is fully insured, with $100,000 of unused capacity.

**Retirement.** Priya's $130,000 IRA CD is tested on its own. It does not touch her $180,000 single-account balance, so she is well inside the limit.

All $865,000 is insured. Their unused capacity at this one bank adds up to $70,000 + $95,000 + $100,000 + $120,000 = $385,000, meaning they could hold $1,250,000 here — $250,000 + $250,000 + $500,000 + $250,000 — before a single dollar became uninsured, with no trust paperwork at all.

Now break it. Suppose Marcus closes the joint account and moves the $400,000 into his own name for convenience. His single category becomes $95,000 + $60,000 + $400,000 = $555,000. Insured: $250,000. Uninsured: $305,000. Same household, same bank, same total money, one signature line different.

Going the other direction: if the couple names their two children as payable-on-death beneficiaries on that joint money market account, the account leaves the joint category and enters the trust category. Coverage becomes 2 owners × 2 beneficiaries × $250,000 = $1,000,000 for that one account. Worth understanding clearly — the account moved, it did not multiply. The joint category no longer covers it at all.

## What Does Not Expand Coverage

- **Opening more accounts in the same category.** Four savings accounts in your sole name share one $250,000 limit.
- **Mixing product types.** A CD, an MMA, and a savings account in the same category still aggregate.
- **Using different branches.** One charter, one set of limits, no matter how many buildings.
- **Using different brand names of the same bank.** Several online brands can operate under one FDIC certificate. Their deposits combine.
- **Adding a beneficiary to a joint account and expecting both categories.** The account changes category; it does not occupy two.
- **Naming the same beneficiary on multiple accounts.** Trust coverage counts unique beneficiaries per owner across all trust deposits at the bank, not per account.
- **Naming an ineligible beneficiary.** A pet, or an entity that is not a person, charity, or nonprofit, does not create coverage.
- **Naming more than five beneficiaries.** The sixth and beyond add nothing.

## Beneficiary Mistakes That Shrink Coverage

The most expensive errors are quiet ones. A beneficiary designation made verbally and never entered into the bank's records does not exist for insurance purposes — the FDIC works from the deposit account records. A beneficiary who has died and was never replaced reduces the count. A trust amended by an attorney but never reported to the bank leaves those records stale.

There is also a timing rule worth knowing. When two insured banks merge, deposits you held at the acquired bank stay separately insured for six months after the merger, and CDs stay separately insured until they mature after that window. If you deliberately split money across two banks and those banks combine, that grace period is your window to rebalance, not a permanent state.

## Verifying With BankFind and EDIE

Two free FDIC tools settle these questions without a phone call.

**BankFind Suite** (banks.data.fdic.gov/bankfind-suite) confirms an institution is FDIC-insured and shows its certificate number along with the trade names operating under that charter. Run this before assuming two brands are two banks — if they share a certificate, you have one limit, not two.

**EDIE**, the Electronic Deposit Insurance Estimator (edie.fdic.gov), takes your actual account list — ownership, balances, beneficiaries — and returns the per-category result with any uninsured amount identified. It produces a printable report, and it is worth redoing after any change in ownership, beneficiaries, or a large deposit. Credit union members need the NCUA's own estimator instead.

## Yield and Coverage as Separate Questions

Structure decides whether the money is protected. Rates decide what it earns. Answer them independently.

As of August 17, 2026, the FDIC national average was 0.38% APY for savings, 0.63% APY for money market accounts, and 1.71% APY for 12-month CDs, with 6-month CDs at 1.41% APY and 60-month CDs at 1.36% APY. These are national averages across thousands of institutions, and online banks commonly pay well above them. Deposit rates move with Federal Reserve policy and with how hard banks are competing for balances — no one can tell you where they go next.

Two practical notes. CDs generally charge an early-withdrawal penalty, so a CD used to fill coverage capacity should hold money you won't need before maturity. And compare APY to APY, since APY reflects compounding and a stated interest rate does not.

## A Coverage Check You Can Finish Today

List every deposit account you hold, grouped by bank. Under each bank, sort the accounts by ownership category rather than by product. Add the balances within each category and compare to $250,000, remembering that posted interest pushes the total up over time. Run BankFind to confirm which brands share a charter. Run EDIE on anything close to a limit.

For most households the fix is not moving to another bank. It is a beneficiary form that was never filed, a joint account that quietly became a single one, or a second brand that turned out to be the same charter — small corrections that change the insured number substantially.

title: Money Market Account vs. Money Market Fund: What's Insured
description: Two products share a name but only one is a deposit account with FDIC coverage; here is how to tell which one holds your emergency fund.
content:
A money market account and a money market fund are separated by one word on the page and by a legal chasm underneath it. The first is a deposit at a bank or credit union, sitting inside the same insurance framework as your checking account. The second is a mutual fund — a pooled investment holding short-term debt that passes the income through to shareholders. Both are conservative products. Only one of them is insured.

That difference rarely announces itself. It surfaces on the day you need the cash in a hurry, or on the day a bank fails and you learn which pile your balance was in. Plenty of people move an emergency fund into something labeled money market without ever checking which of the two they bought.

This post covers three things: what protection sits behind each product, how each behaves under stress, and a short check you can run on your own statement to find out which one you hold.

## Two Names, Two Legal Structures

A money market account (MMA) is a deposit. You hand money to an insured bank or credit union, the institution owes it back, and the FDIC stands behind that obligation up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Credit unions sit outside the FDIC and are covered instead by the NCUA, with the same headline limit. It is a bank product start to finish: a balance, a rate the bank sets, a regulator watching the bank's books.

A money market fund (MMF) is a registered mutual fund. You own shares. The fund owns short-term instruments — Treasury bills, agency paper, repurchase agreements, commercial paper, bank certificates of deposit — and it answers to the SEC, not to bank regulators. No bank promises you anything, and fund materials are required to say so, which is why they carry some version of "Not FDIC insured. No bank guarantee. May lose value."

Held in a brokerage account, a fund does carry one protection that gets routinely misread. SIPC covers up to $500,000 in securities, including $250,000 in cash, if the brokerage firm fails and customer assets go missing. It does not protect against the investment losing value.

## Side by Side

| | Money market account | Money market fund |
|---|---|---|
| What you hold | A deposit; the bank owes you the balance | Shares of a mutual fund |
| Insurance | FDIC or NCUA, $250,000 per depositor, per institution, per ownership category | Not covered; SIPC addresses broker failure, not investment loss |
| Value | A dollar is a dollar | Priced per share; many funds aim to hold $1.00, some price with a floating value |
| Yield source | A rate the institution sets | Portfolio income, minus the fund's expense ratio |
| Getting cash out | Transfer, check, or debit, subject to any limits the bank sets | Sell shares, wait for settlement, then transfer |
| Oversight | Bank and credit union regulators | SEC |

## Behavior Under Stress

### When a bank fails

The failure path for a deposit is well worn. The FDIC takes over and insured balances are made whole — usually within a few business days, often by moving the account to an acquiring institution so the depositor barely notices. Anything above the limit becomes a claim against the receivership, paid from whatever the failed bank's assets recover, on a timeline nobody can promise. The insured portion is the part that behaves predictably.

### When markets seize

A fund doesn't fail; its portfolio either holds up or it doesn't. Two things can go wrong. The first is value: funds that aim to hold a stable share price do it through accounting convention and portfolio discipline, not a guarantee, and in severe conditions a share price can fall below its target. That happened during the 2008 crisis, which prompted emergency government support for the sector. It is rare — and rare is not impossible, which is the exact case an emergency fund exists for.

The second is access. Fund rules permit certain funds to charge liquidity fees when redemptions surge, so the money can still be there while costing something to reach. On an ordinary day none of that applies. Stress is when the two products stop resembling each other.

## The Emergency Fund Problem

An emergency fund has one job: be there, in full, at an unpredictable moment, without requiring you to think. Judged against that job, the naming confusion causes three distinct failures.

- **Uninsured without knowing it.** Someone believes their cash reserve carries deposit insurance when it never did. The belief costs nothing until it is tested.
- **A longer access chain than expected.** Reaching cash in a fund means a sale, a settlement, and then a transfer, all on business days. A deposit balance is already cash, and many MMAs come with checks or a debit card. Regulation D's six-per-month transfer limit was suspended in 2020, though plenty of banks still enforce limits of their own, so read the account terms instead of assuming either way.
- **Yield chasing for pocket change.** As of August 17, 2026, the FDIC national average is 0.63% APY for money market accounts against 0.38% for savings — a gap of 0.25 percentage points. On a $20,000 reserve that is $50 a year, real money but not enough to justify holding emergency cash in something whose value can move.

None of this makes money market funds bad. They are a reasonable home for cash you don't need this week. The mismatch is specific: emergency money wants a deposit.

## A Five-Minute Statement Check

Pull up the account and look for these tells.

**It's a fund if you see:**
- A ticker symbol, typically five letters ending in X
- A share count and a price per share rather than a single balance
- An expense ratio, a prospectus, or a seven-day yield quoted instead of an APY
- Income described as dividends
- A disclosure reading "Not FDIC insured. No bank guarantee. May lose value."

**It's a deposit if you see:**
- "Member FDIC" or "Federally insured by NCUA" on the statement
- One balance, no share count and no price
- Income posted as interest paid
- An APY quoted for the account
- Terms describing transfer limits, minimum balances, or monthly fees

Brokerage accounts deserve extra attention, because uninvested cash there — the sweep — can be either. Some firms sweep into a money market fund; others sweep into deposits at partner banks, where the disclosures name each program bank. Same screen, same "cash" label, two different answers.

When you want confirmation rather than inference, the FDIC's BankFind tool shows whether an institution is insured, and its EDIE calculator runs a specific set of balances through the ownership category rules.

## Coverage Math on a Real Balance

Say you hold $310,000 in a money market account at one bank, in your name alone.

The single ownership category covers $250,000. The remaining $60,000 is uninsured — not lost, not at risk on any ordinary day, just outside the guarantee. A common misreading is to open a second account at the same bank in the same name and assume the coverage doubles. It doesn't. Coverage runs per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so two single-name accounts at one bank share one $250,000 limit.

Ownership categories are the lever that works. A joint account is a separate category, and each co-owner is insured for $250,000 of the joint balance, so a two-person joint account carries up to $500,000. Move the $60,000 there and the arithmetic becomes:

- Single-name account: $250,000, fully insured
- Joint account: $60,000, of which each owner's share is $30,000 — far below the $250,000 per-owner limit, fully insured
- Uninsured: $0

Between two people at that one bank, the ceiling is $250,000 each in single accounts plus $500,000 joint: $1,000,000 without opening a relationship anywhere else.

One more piece of arithmetic catches people. At the 0.63% national average, a $250,000 balance earns about $1,575 over a year, which is roughly $130 a month in credited interest. APY is worth understanding here: it is the figure that already reflects the effect of compounding over a year, while a stated interest rate on its own does not. Park exactly $250,000 and the first month's credit alone carries the balance past the insured limit. Leave a buffer, or move the interest out on a schedule.

## Matching the Product to the Job

Sort your cash by when you'll need it, then pick the structure that fits.

Money you might need this month belongs in a deposit account, where a dollar stays a dollar and insurance does the worrying. Money with a known date and no chance of an early call can go into term deposits — the FDIC national average for a 12-month CD is 1.71% APY as of August 17, 2026, against 0.63% for money market accounts, and that gap is payment for giving up access, enforced by an early-withdrawal penalty if you change your mind. Cash that is genuinely surplus — held for yield rather than availability — is the money a fund can reasonably hold, because you are not counting on it being there in full on one specific bad day.

Confirm what you hold, confirm the insurance is real, confirm the balance sits under the limit in the right ownership category — then stop thinking about it. Getting that right on a quiet day is what keeps it from mattering on a loud one.
